title: How O3DE Lights a Frame
subtitle: O3DE's opaque frame, pass by pass: ported to WGSL and read from O3DE's source

chapters.title: O3DE's opaque frame
chapters.summary: The forward pixel shader, its targets, and the passes that follow it.

beats.headline: One light, one material
narration: This is the Open 3D Engine's Atom renderer, lighting the lab's study room with the shaders of its StandardPBR material, ported to WGSL.

narration.text: One light hangs in the room: a simple point light, O3DE's plainest punctual light, with no shape and no shadows.
Every formula you will see comes from O3DE version two point eight, read straight from its source.

narration: Each surface here is lit twice.

narration.text: Once by the point light, in the forward pass, and once by the sky, in passes that run after it.

beats.headline: A pixel's path through the frame
narration: Here is the path one pixel takes through the frame.

narration.text: A depth pre-pass draws the scene's depth first, and light culling sorts the lights into screen tiles.
The forward pass applies decals, evaluates the material and its lights, and writes diffuse and specular light into two separate targets.
It also writes albedo times the diffuse response, the specular colour with the roughness, and the normal, which later passes read back.
Full-screen passes then add the sky's diffuse light and the reflections, from the sky and from reflection probes; SSAO darkens the diffuse, and a merge pass adds the two together.
In pseudo-code, the forward pixel shader is short.
It evaluates the surface from the material's inputs, and initialises the lighting data.
Then it adds the lights listed for the pixel's screen tile: directional lights, then simple point and spot lights, then area lights. This room has one simple point light.
Here, image-based lighting runs only for transparent materials, or for specular when a mesh or material asks for it; opaque ones get it from full-screen passes.
Diffuse and specular end up in separate targets, and the merge pass sums them.
Let's take the result apart.
This is the point light's diffuse lighting on its own.
This is its specular lighting: small, sharp highlights, brightest on the floor below the light.
And this is everything together, with the sky's light added by the passes after the forward pass.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: These are the functions this chapter followed.
Every claim in this video cites a file, a symbol, and a line in the O3DE checkout, and the build checks each line is still there.

chapters.title: Light culling
chapters.summary: Tiles, depth bins, and the lists the forward pass walks.

narration.text: That was the whole frame; the next part looks at its first lighting step, light culling.
Before the forward pass, O3DE decides which lights each part of the screen needs.
Here, twenty-four small simple point lights hang over the room; a dot marks each one.
The screen is cut into tiles of sixteen by sixteen pixels, and each tile gets its own list of lights.
In false colour, each pixel shows how many lights its tile keeps at its depth: dark blue for none, yellow for eight or more.
Three compute passes build these lists, after a depth pre-pass and before any shading.
The first, LightCullingTilePrepare, runs one thread per pixel and one group per tile.
It finds the tile's nearest depth, and its farthest one short of the sky, opaque and transparent alike, so a wall seen against the sky stays shallow.
It marks a thirty-two-slice mask between them, one bit for each slice that holds a surface.
And it splits the range into one, two, four, or eight depth bins, from the base-two log of its span in metres.
The box drawn here is the inspected point's tile in view space, with its bins as slices.
The second pass, LightCulling, tests each light against each tile.
A light is kept when its sphere touches the tile's box, and its depth range touches a filled slice of the mask.
Each kept light is written as its index, shifted sixteen bits, with one bit for each depth bin it reaches.
Lights are grouped by type, decals first, then simple point lights, spot lights, and the area lights, each group closed by an end marker.
O3DE's threads append a group's lights in whatever order they finish, decals excepted, since those are sorted; the lab appends lights in index order, so its frames never change.
As the lights' radius grows, more tiles keep them.
The third pass, LightCullingRemap, rewrites each tile's list as one list per depth bin.
The forward pass finds the bin at its own depth, and walks only that list.
At the inspected point, the readout counts the lights in the tile's list, those its bin keeps, and those whose spheres reach the point.
The ringed dots are the lights the point's bin keeps, each joined to the point by a dashed line.
Now the lights move: as each one crosses tiles and depth bins, the colours and the point's list follow it.
The lab compares every tile's list on the GPU with a CPU copy, and checks that no light reaching a surface is missing from its bin.

beats.headline: A light type that never shades

narration.text: One finding: the forward pass also walks a group for polygon lights.
But the culling pass writes no such group, so with light culling on, which is the default, polygon lights never shade anything.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: These entries follow the three culling passes, the tile iterator, and the polygon-light finding.

chapters.title: The surface
chapters.summary: The metallic workflow and the roughness remap.

narration.text: With the lights sorted into lists, the next part turns to what they light: the surface.
Every lighting function starts from the same surface record.
The material provides a base colour, a metallic value, a specular F zero factor, and a roughness.
From these, O3DE derives what the lighting actually uses.
Albedo is the base colour times one minus metallic, so a metal has no diffuse colour at all.
Specular F zero blends from a dielectric value to the base colour as metallic grows.
The dielectric value is zero point zero eight times the factor, so the default factor of one half gives zero point zero four, the reflectance of most paint and plastic.
Metallic values between zero and one blend the two, which suits only transitions such as dust on metal.
Roughness is authored on a perceptual scale.
O3DE clamps it to at least zero point zero two four, squares it into alpha, and squares it again.
So a roughness of one half becomes an alpha squared of one sixteenth, before anti-aliasing widens it.
Watch the sphere as roughness sweeps from polished to matte.
Then specular anti-aliasing, on by default, widens alpha squared where the normal turns quickly from pixel to pixel.
It adds a kernel of half the squared change in the normal across and down a pixel, never more than zero point one eight.
Then it recomputes alpha and the linear roughness from the result, so every later term sees the wider lobe.
On a smooth sphere the widening shows toward the rim, where the normal turns fastest across a pixel.
The lab takes those derivatives as O3DE does, from the fine screen-space derivatives of the normal.
A material can also carry two occlusion maps: diffuse ambient occlusion, and specular occlusion, sometimes called a cavity map.
Each is the map's red channel, raised to the power of its factor, which defaults to one.
Without a map, both are one, and nothing changes.
At the end of the forward pass, diffuse light is multiplied by the ambient occlusion, and specular light by the specular occlusion.
The albedo target carries both on to the skylight's passes, with the specular occlusion in its alpha.
Raising the factor deepens the creases; lowering it toward zero fades the map out.

beats.headline: Every object, the same rules
narration: The same rules apply to every object in the room.

narration.text: Make the teapot metal, and its green leaves the diffuse light and moves into the highlight.
Make the box rough, and its highlight spreads until it is barely there.
Each of them goes through the same two functions before any light is evaluated.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: The surface comes from these four places: the material's evaluation, the metallic workflow, its constants, and the roughness remap.

chapters.title: Decals
chapters.summary: Box-projected textures blended into the surface before lighting.

narration.text: Before any light reaches that surface, decals can change it, and they are the next part.
Decals project a texture onto whatever surfaces fall inside a box.
Here, a paint splat and a panel grid lie on the floor; the boxes and arrows show their volumes and projection axes.
Decals are on by default, and they change the surface itself, before the lighting data is set up.
So every light, and the skylight's passes after the forward pass, see the decal's albedo, F zero, and normal.
ApplyDecal moves the point into the decal's box, through its rotation and its half size, and skips it outside minus one to one.
The box's x and y become the texture coordinates, with v flipped.
The base map times the decal's colour replaces the albedo, by the map's alpha times the decal's opacity and its angle fade.
F zero moves too, by that amount times metallic, so a decal on metal changes the colour it reflects.
And its normal map bends the normal, here into the grooves between the panels.
The normal map's two channels are swapped back and its z is rebuilt, as for any O3DE normal map.
Each decal fades with the angle between the surface and its projection axis.
The cosine is clamped at zero point five five and smoothstepped to one, so a decal is gone by about fifty-seven degrees.
Tilting the splat's axis away from the floor's normal fades it out.
The attenuation-angle setting, one by default, blends between none of that fade and all of it.
Where decals overlap, their order decides which one lands on top.
Light culling puts decals in the first group of each tile's list, as spheres around their boxes.
Then it sorts them by sort key, and by index where keys are equal, so a larger key is applied later and wins.
The grid keeps the default key of sixteen, and the splat has seventeen, so the splat lies over the grid.
Give the splat fifteen, and the grid covers it.
The forward pass walks that sorted group before it sets up any lighting.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: These entries show where decals enter the forward pass, how each one is blended, and how they are culled and sorted.

chapters.title: GGX specular
chapters.summary: N, L, V, and H; the D, G, and F terms; the specular lobe.

narration.text: With the surface ready, the next part is how each light's highlight is computed: GGX specular.
Specular lighting depends on four directions at one point.
The surface normal, N.
The direction to the light, L.
The direction to the viewer, V; we look from the blue observer, so that all four lie in a plane facing us.
And the half vector, H, halfway between L and V.
A microfacet whose normal points along H mirrors the light straight into the viewer.
SpecularGGX multiplies three terms, D, G, and F, with N dot L and the multiscatter compensation.
D, the GGX normal distribution, is the density of microfacet normals that point along H; for a smooth surface it rises far above one.
In false colour, D is bright only where H meets the normal: the core of the highlight.
G is the height-correlated Smith term: the share of those facets that are neither shadowed nor hidden.
O3DE returns it already divided by four, N dot L, and N dot V, which saves the division at the end.
F is Schlick's Fresnel, taken on H dot V: reflectance rises toward white as the light and the view graze the microfacet.
That product is the specular response; times the light's intensity, it is the specular lighting.
Now the numbers at the point, and its lobe.
The pink curve is the specular response for every outgoing direction in this plane, and it leans around the mirror direction of L.
Raise the light toward the normal, and the lobe stands up with it.
Lower it toward the horizon: N dot L falls, Fresnel grows, and the lobe stretches out.
The readout follows every term as the light moves.
Roughness changes D more than anything else.
A smooth surface concentrates its light into a tall, narrow lobe and a small, bright highlight.
A rough one spreads the same light thin.
In false colour, D grows from a pinpoint to a broad glow.
SpecularGGX and its three terms live in three short files of O3DE's shader library.

chapters.title: Clear coat
chapters.summary: A dielectric layer over the base: its F zero, diffuse, specular, and IBL.

narration.text: The next part puts a second specular layer over GGX: clear coat.
Clear coat adds a thin, clear layer over the base material, like varnish over paint.
It is off by default; here the sphere is a rough metal under a smooth coat.
The coat is a dielectric with an F zero of four percent, and its own factor and roughness.
Under the coat, the base's F zero changes, because light now enters it from the coat rather than from air.
O3DE uses Filament's form: one minus five root F zero, over five minus root F zero, squared, blended in by the factor.
The diffuse response shrinks by the coat's Fresnel at the view angle.
And each light's diffuse shrinks again, by the coat's Fresnel at the half vector.
A finding: the coat dims diffuse light twice, once through the response and once per light.
Each light's specular becomes the base lobe, times one minus the coat's Fresnel, plus the coat's own lobe.
The coat's lobe is GGX with Kelemen's visibility term, at an alpha of its roughness squared, never below zero point zero zero zero five.
So the sphere shows a sharp highlight from the coat, on top of the metal's broad one.
As the factor rises, the sharp highlight grows, and the metal's colour dims beneath it.

beats.headline: The sky's reflection, in the forward pass

narration.text: Clear coat also moves the material's sky reflections into the forward pass.
The full-screen reflection pass knows nothing of the coat, so the mesh is drawn without the specular-IBL stencil value, and that pass skips it.
In the forward pass, the base's reflection is scaled by one minus the coat's Fresnel, squared, and the coat's own reflection is added.
So the full-screen probe passes never touch a clear-coated mesh; instead the forward pass blends in the smallest probe that overlaps it, between its inner and outer boxes.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: These entries follow the coat from its inputs to its specular, its diffuse, and its forward-pass IBL.

chapters.title: Diffuse and its response
chapters.summary: Lambertian diffuse, scaled by one minus a roughness-aware Fresnel; Disney diffuse compared.

narration.text: From specular, the next part turns to the other half of each light: diffuse, and its response.
Diffuse light in StandardPBR is Lambertian: albedo, times N dot L, over pi.
But it is scaled by a diffuse response: one minus a Fresnel term at the view angle.
That Fresnel knows the roughness: its grazing value is one minus roughness, but never less than F zero.
So a smooth surface seen at a grazing angle keeps less of its light for diffuse, because more of it goes to specular.
Without that response, diffuse and specular together could send back more light than arrives.
In false colour, the diffuse response stays near one, and dips only toward the sphere's rim.
The green lobe shows the result for every view direction: nearly a half circle, flattened where the response falls.
Smoother surfaces dip more at grazing angles.

beats.headline: A diffuse model StandardPBR does not use

narration.text: O3DE's BRDF library also defines a normalized Disney diffuse.
StandardPBR never calls it; the Skin material does, and EnhancedPBR does when subsurface scattering is on.
It carries its own Fresnel terms for light entering and leaving the surface, so it takes no diffuse response.
Back to the Lambertian model that StandardPBR uses.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: These entries show the diffuse term, its response, and which materials use the Disney model.

chapters.title: Transmission (EnhancedPBR)
chapters.summary: Light through thick and thin objects, and the point light it needs.

narration.text: So far light has only bounced off surfaces; the next part lets it pass through them: transmission.
Thin or translucent things, like leaves, wax, or skin, let light through from behind.
StandardPBR has no transmission; EnhancedPBR adds it, off by default, with a thick-object and a thin-object mode.
Its other lighting is StandardPBR's, as long as subsurface scattering and anisotropy stay off.
Here the teapot is EnhancedPBR, lit from behind; the simple point light is off.

beats.headline: A different kind of point light

narration.text: Simple point lights add no back lighting at all.
So the light behind the teapot is O3DE's point light, a sphere area light, with the editor's default radius of five centimetres.
It lights like a simple point light, but moves its specular direction to the point of its bulb nearest the reflection ray, and adds back lighting.
Here it casts no shadows.
Thick mode follows Barré-Brisebois and Bouchard: how directly the light shines through toward the viewer.
The view direction is compared with the light's direction bent by the normal, raised to a power of six, and scaled.
Then it is attenuated through the thickness: e to the minus four times the thickness, times one minus the thickness.
The thickness is the larger of the shadow map's and the material's; this teapot uses zero point one five, where the default is one half.
The sum over lights, times the tint, joins the diffuse light after the occlusion multiply, so occlusion never dims it.
Without transmission the teapot's back is dark; with it, the light glows through.
Thin mode follows Jimenez and others: a diffusion profile over the distance the shadow map measures through the object.
Its comment says that without shadow data it gives no back lighting.
A finding: for point lights, the shadow branch runs even for a light without shadows, because its options default to true.
There the shadow lookup returns a thickness of zero, not the negative value that means no data.
So a thin object behind a shadowless point light gets the kernel's full value, the brightest back lighting it can have.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: These entries cover transmission's inputs, the sphere light, both modes, and the shadow-branch finding.

chapters.title: The BRDF texture and multiscatter
chapters.summary: BRDFTextureCS, the energy single scattering loses, and the compensation.

beats.headline: Energy that single scattering loses

narration.text: The next part returns to specular, and to the BRDF texture that O3DE fills at startup.

narration: A single GGX bounce loses energy on rough surfaces.
Light that strikes one microfacet can bounce to another before it escapes, and the single-scattering formula simply drops it.

narration.text: Here is a rough metal sphere with that loss left in.
And here it is with O3DE's compensation: brighter, as a real rough metal would be.
To know how much is lost, O3DE fills a two hundred fifty six by two hundred fifty six texture, two sixteen-bit floats per texel, once at startup; the lab keeps it in thirty-two-bit floats.
Each texel stands for one view angle and one roughness.
It draws one thousand and twenty four GGX samples, reflects the view about each, and weights those above the horizon by the visibility times four, V dot H, and N dot L, over N dot H.
It splits the sum into a scale A and a bias B on F zero.
The rows are stored upside down, so lighting looks the texture up by smoothness rather than roughness.
A plus B is the energy that single scattering keeps.
At roughness zero point eight and this view angle, that is only about fifty seven percent.
The compensation adds the missing part back, in proportion to F zero, following Turquin's method.
Its shader option defaults to on, but StandardPBR's material property defaults to off, so a material must turn it on, as O3DE's metal presets do; the lab turns it on.
In false colour, the compensation grows with roughness.

beats.headline: A detail of the texture shader

narration.text: One detail of the texture shader stood out when it was ported.
Its sampler takes the square root of one minus cos theta squared, without a guard.

narration: On the GPU used for this lab, cos theta can round above one for an almost mirror-like lobe; the square root then gives not a number, and the sample is lost.
So the WGSL port loses energy below a roughness of about zero point zero three.
The lab fills its texture on the CPU instead; whether O3DE's own texture shows the loss depends on the GPU.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: The texture's shader, its size, how lighting reads it, and the compensation are in these files.

chapters.title: The simple point light
chapters.summary: Inverse square, the radius window, no shadows, the automatic radius.

beats.headline: A position, an intensity, a radius

narration.text: So far the light itself has been a given; the next part looks at the simple point light.
A simple point light stores a position, an RGB intensity in candelas, one over its attenuation radius squared, and its lighting channels and GI flags.
Its intensity falls off with the inverse square of distance: the dashed curve on the floor.
Then a window pulls it smoothly to zero at the attenuation radius: the solid curve.
The window is one minus the squared ratio of distance squared to radius squared, all squared once more.
At half the radius it still keeps eighty eight percent, so the solid curve follows the dashed one closely and drops only near the edge.
The readout follows one point on the sphere: its distance, the falloff ratio, the window, and the illuminance that reaches it.
Six candelas at just under two metres give about one point seven lux, before the window.
Beyond the radius, the light is skipped entirely, so the radius also limits its cost.
Grow the radius, and the window reaches further.
In the automatic mode, the default, the radius is the square root of the light's lumens, weighted by its colour's luminance, over zero point one.
Lights and meshes also carry lighting channels: five bits each.
A light shades a surface only when their masks share a bit.
Components start with all five channels set, so by default every light reaches every mesh.
Give the light a mask of one and the sphere a mask of two, and the sphere stops receiving it.
The skylight, the reflection passes, and decals ignore the channels.
A finding: in the directional-light loop, a light of another channel ends the whole loop, so the directional lights after it are skipped too.

beats.headline: No shadows

narration.text: Simple point lights cast no shadows.

narration: Light reaches every surface that faces it, even behind the boxes.

narration.text: With no shadow maps, and culled per screen tile, each one costs little more than shading the pixels inside its radius.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: The light's record, its falloff, the loop that skips it, and the automatic radius are listed here.

chapters.title: The global skylight
chapters.summary: Offline GGX and cosine prefiltering; the two full-screen passes; no occlusion.

beats.headline: Light from the sky

narration.text: That covers the simple point light; the next part leaves punctual lights behind.

narration: The second source of light is the sky.

narration.text: O3DE's global skylight is image-based lighting: an environment, stored as two cubemaps.
This chrome sphere reflects it directly; it is the lab's own sky, with a warm softbox high on one side.

beats.headline: Baked offline
narration: The cubemaps are baked offline, by O3DE's image processor.

narration.text: A GGX filter turns the environment into a specular cubemap with two hundred fifty six texel faces in R9G9B9E5, and six mips, one for each step of roughness.
A cosine filter turns it into a diffuse cubemap of thirty two to one hundred twenty eight texels a face; the lab's is thirty two.

narration: And, separately, the BRDF texture from chapter five supplies the split-sum terms.

narration.text: Mip m of the specular cubemap is filtered for a roughness of m over five.
For each texel, the filter assumes that the normal and the view both point along the texel's direction.
Then it takes two hundred fifty six GGX samples around it.
Each sample is read one mip blurrier than the mip whose texels match its solid angle, blended between two mips, which hides the noise of so few samples.
Rougher mips gather a wider cone, so reflections blur.
The diffuse cubemap is a cosine-weighted average over the whole hemisphere, normalised by its weights.
So it stores irradiance divided by pi, and the diffuse pass multiplies it by albedo with no division.
Seen alone, the diffuse light from the sky is soft, and coloured by the ground below and the blue above.
At run time, the forward pass has already stored albedo times the diffuse response and occlusion, F zero, and roughness, each in eight bits.
The diffuse pass multiplies that albedo by the diffuse cubemap at the normal.
The reflection pass reads the specular cubemap along the reflection vector, at mip roughness times five.
It applies the split sum, F zero times A plus B, with the compensation and N dot V held at one hundredth or more, then the skylight's exposure and the specular occlusion.
The diffuse pass adds straight onto the diffuse target; the reflection pass writes its own target, which a composite pass adds onto the specular one.
At the inspected point, the readout shows each step: the eight-bit roughness, its mip, the prefiltered light, and the split sum.
As roughness rises, the mip rises with it, and the reflection dims and spreads.
The global skylight casts no shadows: only occlusion maps and screen-space ambient occlusion, which is on by default, dim it.
The lab's room has no occlusion maps, so inside it only SSAO darkens the sky's light, in the corners and under the objects.
For interiors, O3DE replaces the sky's reflections with reflection probes, in the next chapter, and its diffuse light with a diffuse probe grid, which the lab leaves out.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: The bake, the targets, and the two passes are in these files; CubeMapGen, the filter library, is AMD's, under a BSD license.

chapters.title: Reflection probes
chapters.summary: Probe cubemaps, their stencil and blend weights, parallax, and the composite.

narration.text: The sky's cubemaps light the whole scene alike; the next part, reflection probes, gives places reflections of their own.
Inside a room, reflections of an open sky look wrong: the walls should be in them.
Reflection probes fix that: each is a cubemap baked from a point in the scene, with an inner and an outer box.
The lab places two, and bakes them itself on the CPU, shading the room from each probe's centre.
Their cubemaps have two hundred fifty-six texels a face, as the default Medium bake quality makes them, and are prefiltered like the sky's.
On the glossy floor, the probes put the room's own walls into the reflections.
Five passes run after the forward pass: a stencil pass, a blend-weight pass, the global pass, and an outer and an inner probe pass.
The stencil pass draws each probe's inner box, slightly reduced, and adds one to the stencil of every surface inside it that uses the reflection passes.
Surfaces outside every inner box keep the value three.
There, the blend-weight pass adds each probe's weight: one at its inner box, falling to zero at its outer one.
Where probes overlap, the weights add up.
The global pass then runs only outside the inner boxes, and keeps what the probes leave: one minus their summed weight, at most one.
The outer pass adds each probe's reflection times its weight, divided by the total wherever that exceeds one.
Inside an inner box, the inner pass simply replaces the reflection with the probe's.
Probes are drawn largest first, so a smaller probe inside a larger one has the last word.
Unlike the global pass, the probes apply no specular occlusion.
Shrinking the inner boxes widens the bands where probes blend.
A cubemap is captured from one point, but surfaces are everywhere in the box.
So by default the reflection ray is traced to the outer box, and the cubemap is read toward that hit from the probe's centre.
Without that correction, the reflected walls slide out of place.
The composite pass then adds the reflection target onto the specular light, wherever the stencil marks a surface.
A finding: that target is cleared to a grey of zero point four, and the global pass never runs inside the inner boxes.
So with image-based lighting switched off, the inner pass discards, and surfaces inside an inner box get that grey added to their specular.
The lab reproduces it, as its readout shows.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: These entries follow the five reflection passes in order, the probe's specular, and the composite.

chapters.title: Ambient occlusion
chapters.summary: SSAO at half resolution: samples, blur, upsample, and the diffuse multiply.

narration.text: The last part before the recap is ambient occlusion.
Light from the sky reaches into corners and creases as brightly as onto open floor.
Screen-space ambient occlusion darkens those places from the depth buffer alone, and the main pipeline runs it by default.
It runs after the reflections and subsurface scattering, and multiplies only the diffuse target, direct light and sky alike.
This is its result, white where nothing occludes.
It starts from linear depth: the view-space depth of each pixel's first MSAA sample.
Then it works at half resolution, keeping the upper-left pixel of every two by two.
SsaoCompute rebuilds each pixel's position and normal from depth, and gathers fifty-two samples around it: twelve close by, and ten rotations of four shared with its neighbours.
Each sample adds the cosine between the normal and the direction to it, weighted by one over its squared distance plus zero point zero seven, and the occlusion is their weighted average.
The result is one minus the occlusion times the strength, raised to the power two point two, and stored in eight bits.
The strength defaults to one, and the sampling radius to five percent of the half-resolution height.
A wider radius reaches farther and darkens more broadly.
The raw result is noisy, so a depth-aware blur smooths it, down and then across.
It runs from pixel to pixel, keeping two thirds of the value before, and less where the depth's slope changes, so edges stay sharp.
Each output is half the chain from eight pixels before it and half the chain from eight after.
Those values are the blur pass's own defaults, used when the scene has no ambient-occlusion component; the component's are zero point eight five and two hundred.
Without the blur, the samples' pattern shows through.
DepthUpsample brings it back to full resolution from the four nearest half-resolution pixels, weighted by distance and by how close their depths are.
Then the diffuse target is multiplied by it, and the merge pass adds the specular light, untouched.
The lab checks each of these stages on the GPU against a CPU copy, to within one eight-bit step.
Because it only sees depth, SSAO knows nothing of what lies off screen or behind the nearest surface.

beats.headline: Where to read
narration: These entries follow SSAO from the linear depth through the samples, the blur, and the upsample to the diffuse multiply.

chapters.title: Recap
chapters.summary: What StandardPBR does, and what the lab leaves out.

beats.headline: The opaque frame, in summary

narration.text: That is every part; here is how they fit together.
To recap: this is O3DE's opaque frame, pass by pass.

Light culling sorts the lights into tiles; the forward pass applies decals, then each light, with GGX specular, clear coat where enabled, a Lambertian diffuse scaled by its response, and transmission for EnhancedPBR.
Full-screen passes then add the skylight and the reflection probes, read back from eight-bit targets, and SSAO darkens the diffuse before the merge.

narration: The lab ports these formulas to WGSL, checks each one against a CPU copy, and cites every line it follows.

narration.text: It leaves out shadows, area and directional lights, screen-space reflections, which are off by default, and the diffuse probe grid.
